title: Project Valhalla's First Preview: JEP 401 Redefines == for Java Objects
gist: JEP 401 (Value Objects) has landed as a preview in JDK 28, introducing a `value` class modifier whose instances have no identity, implicitly final fields, and a redefined `==` that compares field values recursively. It is Project Valhalla's first shipped increment after years of valhalla-dev discussion, and its payoff is JVM scalarization and flattening rather than any guaranteed benchmark gain.

insights.claim: JEP 401, Value Objects, has been integrated into JDK 28 as a preview that is disabled by default and requires --enable-preview at both compile time and run time.
insights.speaker: A N M Bazlur Rahman
insights.so_what: Preview-gated and dual-flagged means near-zero production adoption in the JDK 28 cycle — the real enterprise impact lands two or more releases out.
insights.locator: JEP 401, Value Objects (Preview), has been integrated

insights.claim: The proposal reached integration only after years of discussion on OpenJDK's valhalla-dev mailing list, making it one of the longest-gestating changes to Java's object model.
insights.speaker: A N M Bazlur Rahman
insights.so_what: The long gestation signals the design is unlikely to be reversed — treat value objects as a durable direction for the JVM ecosystem.
insights.quote: The proposal has been shaped by years of discussion on OpenJDK's valhalla-dev mailing list.
insights.locator: For developers, the immediate consequences

insights.claim: JEP 401 depends on a companion change, JEP 539 Strict Field Initialization in the JVM, which supplies the bytecode verification enforcing that every field is assigned before a value instance can be observed.
insights.speaker: A N M Bazlur Rahman
insights.so_what: Value objects required a verifier-level change, meaning tooling that reads or generates bytecode (agents, instrumentation, frameworks) must be updated in lockstep.
insights.locator: Records can take the modifier too

insights.claim: For value objects, == now succeeds when both operands are instances of the same class with the same field values, with reference-typed fields compared recursively using ==; identity objects keep their existing behavior.
insights.speaker: A N M Bazlur Rahman
insights.so_what: The most-taught invariant in Java (== means identity) now depends on a class modifier — expect a wave of subtle bugs and static-analysis rule updates.
insights.quote: For value objects, it succeeds when both operands are instances of the same class with the same field values; reference-typed fields are compared recursively using ==.
insights.locator: The most visible semantic change is ==

insights.claim: Two value objects remain indistinguishable even when upcast to Object, so the new == equality holds through the Object reference type rather than only at the declared value type.
insights.speaker: A N M Bazlur Rahman
insights.so_what: Collections, caches, and identity maps keyed on Object references will silently change behavior for migrated types.
insights.locator: Object o1 = p1, o2 = p2;

insights.claim: String deliberately remains an identity class, so new String(s1) still yields a reference that is != to the original despite equal contents.
insights.speaker: A N M Bazlur Rahman
insights.so_what: The most common == pitfall in Java is unchanged — migration surprises will cluster in wrapper and date types instead.
insights.locator: String s1 = "hamburger";

insights.claim: The JEP explicitly does not position == as a replacement for equals, because a value object's internal state is not always the same as the state it represents.
insights.speaker: A N M Bazlur Rahman
insights.so_what: Guidance stays 'use equals' — teams that read the headline and switch to == will introduce correctness bugs in types with normalized or cached internal state.
insights.quote: JEP 401 does not redefine == as a replacement for equals; the usual advice to compare objects using equals still applies because a value object's internal state is not always the same as the state it represents.
insights.locator: This is not an invitation to abandon equals

insights.claim: A class declared with the new value modifier has implicitly final instance fields and requires every field to be assigned before the instance can be observed; all other classes remain identity classes.
insights.speaker: A N M Bazlur Rahman
insights.so_what: Opt-in via modifier means the migration cost sits with library authors, not the runtime — adoption will track how fast major libraries annotate their small types.
insights.locator: A class declared with the value modifier

insights.claim: Records can also carry the value modifier, as in value record Color(byte red, byte green, byte blue), combining the record's data-carrier syntax with identity-free semantics.
insights.speaker: A N M Bazlur Rahman
insights.so_what: Records become the natural on-ramp to value semantics — existing record-heavy codebases can adopt Valhalla benefits with a one-word diff.
insights.locator: Records can take the modifier too

insights.claim: Instance methods of a value class may not be synchronized, removing a locking capability that existing code may rely on when types migrate to value classes.
insights.speaker: A N M Bazlur Rahman
insights.so_what: Any code synchronizing on primitive wrappers or LocalDate instances breaks under preview — a concrete audit item for concurrency-heavy codebases.
insights.locator: Records can take the modifier too

themes.theme: Migration hazards for existing JDK classes

insights.claim: With preview enabled, several value-based JDK classes including the primitive wrappers and LocalDate become value classes, while with preview disabled the compiler keeps their identity-object forms and behavior stays aligned with JDK 27.
insights.speaker: A N M Bazlur Rahman
insights.so_what: The same source compiles to different semantics depending on a flag — build-configuration drift becomes a correctness risk, not just a portability one.
insights.locator: With preview features enabled, several value-based JDK classes

insights.claim: Creating a Reference for a value object throws IdentityException, breaking APIs such as weak and soft reference usage for migrated types.
insights.speaker: A N M Bazlur Rahman
insights.so_what: Cache and interning libraries built on weak references against wrapper or date types will throw at runtime — a specific breakage class to test for.
insights.quote: creating a Reference for a value object throws IdentityException
insights.locator: Recompilation is recommended for migrated classes

insights.claim: Recompilation is recommended for migrated classes because the LoadableDescriptors class-file attribute is what tells the JVM at load time that a class is a value class.
insights.speaker: A N M Bazlur Rahman
insights.so_what: Pre-compiled binaries and vendored jars will not get the optimization without a rebuild — a real constraint on realizing Valhalla's performance promise in enterprise stacks.
insights.locator: Recompilation is recommended for migrated classes

themes.theme: Performance is an opportunity, not a guarantee

insights.claim: The expected payoff is optimization rather than a guaranteed benchmark result: the JVM may scalarize a value object into constituent fields or flatten it into a compact representation stored directly in a field or array element.
insights.speaker: A N M Bazlur Rahman
insights.so_what: Anyone modeling Valhalla as a step-change in Java throughput is overreaching — the gain is conditional on JIT behavior and data layout.
insights.quote: The expected payoff is optimization rather than a guaranteed benchmark result.
insights.locator: The expected payoff is optimization

insights.claim: Flattening is constrained by atomicity, and on typical platforms the available encoding may be as small as 64 bits including a null flag, capping which value types can actually be flattened.
insights.speaker: A N M Bazlur Rahman
insights.so_what: A 64-bit-with-null-flag budget means multi-field value types largely miss the flattening win — the benefit skews to very small types like points and colors.
insights.quote: on typical platforms, the available encoding may be as small as 64 bits including a null flag
insights.locator: Flattening remains constrained by atomicity

insights.claim: When neither scalarization nor flattening applies, the JVM falls back to ordinary allocation, particularly during warmup before optimized JIT code is available.
insights.speaker: A N M Bazlur Rahman
insights.so_what: Short-lived and serverless JVM workloads may see none of the benefit — the win concentrates in long-running services that reach steady-state JIT.
insights.locator: When neither optimization applies

insights.claim: The if_acmpeq bytecode gains an additional value-object check, with the identity case intended to remain a fast path.
insights.speaker: A N M Bazlur Rahman
insights.so_what: Reference comparison — one of the hottest operations in the JVM — takes on new work; watch for regression reports on identity-heavy workloads.
insights.locator: The JEP acknowledges that value objects make significant changes

insights.claim: JEP 401 frames the underlying problem as a mismatch between developer intent and Java's guarantees: small data-carrying classes like a complex number, pixel color, or date gain identity they never wanted, which the JEP argues is often irrelevant and can be harmful.
insights.speaker: A N M Bazlur Rahman
insights.so_what: The framing — identity as an unwanted default rather than a feature — is the reusable mental model for judging future JVM and language design moves.
insights.quote: For such types, the JEP argues, identity is often irrelevant and can be harmful.
insights.locator: JEP 401 frames the problem as a mismatch

insights.claim: Identity carries a runtime cost because it generally forces the JVM to allocate memory per object and dereference that location on every use, increasing garbage-collector pressure and degrading locality.
insights.speaker: A N M Bazlur Rahman
insights.so_what: GC pressure and cache locality are the mechanism to watch — the benefit shows up in allocation rates and pause behavior, not raw CPU benchmarks.
insights.locator: Identity also carries a run-time cost

insights.claim: Escape analysis is an inadequate substitute because its optimizations are unpredictable and stop helping once an object escapes, including when stored in a field or array.
insights.speaker: A N M Bazlur Rahman
insights.so_what: This is the direct rebuttal to 'the JIT already handles this' — escape analysis fails exactly where data structures live, which is where the cost concentrates.
insights.quote: Escape analysis recovers some of that cost, but its optimizations are unpredictable and do not help once an object escapes, including when it is stored in a field or array.
insights.locator: Escape analysis recovers some of that cost

insights.claim: The JEP concedes value objects make significant changes to Java's object model and that developers may be surprised by the new == and synchronized behavior, while expecting such disruptions to be uncommon and manageable.
insights.speaker: A N M Bazlur Rahman
insights.so_what: The 'uncommon and manageable' claim is the key untested assumption — if wrong, it becomes the drag on JDK 28+ adoption in large enterprises.
insights.locator: The JEP acknowledges that value objects make significant changes

insights.claim: Two security considerations are identified: == and identityHashCode may indirectly expose private field values, and comparing two large trees of value objects may take unbounded time.
insights.speaker: A N M Bazlur Rahman
insights.so_what: Recursive == on deep value trees is an algorithmic-complexity denial-of-service vector in any code comparing untrusted inputs — a concrete new attack surface.
insights.quote: == and identityHashCode may indirectly expose private field values, and comparing two large trees of value objects may take unbounded time
insights.locator: The document identifies two security considerations

insights.claim: javac extends its identity warnings to value classes in JDK 28, giving developers a compile-time signal for identity-sensitive operations on the new types.
insights.speaker: A N M Bazlur Rahman
insights.so_what: Compiler warnings are the main migration safety net — teams should treat identity warnings as errors before enabling the preview broadly.
insights.locator: Some APIs stop working
